args.text:
Take getting up in the morning, for instance. Now, if it's a big house-party, no worries, cos you can always hear the others pattering about and brushing their teeth. You just time your own getting up by how many people seem to be up and about. But if you're the only guest, there's every chance of a frightful mix-up.

"What time's brekkie?" you ask.

"Oh, any old time on Sundays," says the hostess, with a big generous wave. "Sleep in as long as you like. This is 'Liberty Hall.'"

It's a lovely thought, and all, but there's nothing in it you can actually get hold of. It does the trick at the time, but come morning it's that vague it's downright terrifying.

So say you wake up at eight. You listen, and there's no one stirring. Back over onto the cool pillow till twenty past. Then up on your elbow again, head cocked to one side. There's a creak from over near the stairs. They might all be up and heading down to breakfast! Takes you about two seconds to jump out of bed and listen at the door. Maybe you open it a polite crack and have a squiz out. Dead silence, broken only, as they say, by the ticking of the hall clock, and not a soul in sight. They probably just sleep in. Maybe eleven o'clock's their Sunday getting-up time. Some people _are_ like that.

Shut the door and sit on the edge of the bed. No chance of any more sleep now. May as well have a look at the pictures in the guest room, just to pass the time. Here's one of Lorna Doone. How d'e do, Lorna? Here's a group shot--taken in 1902--of your host in evening clothes, hanging onto a mandolin. Probably in his uni musical club. Pretty scruffy-looking mob, you _must_ say. Well, what about this one? An etching of some dodgy-looking barges on what's probably the Thames. Fair enough, I s'pose.

Back to the door for another listen. Tick-tock-tick-tock. If you ran your bath, you'd probably wake the whole house. Better sit back down on the edge of the bed.

Hello, there's some books on the table. "Fifty Famous Sonnets," illustrated by Maxfield Parrish. Never touch a sonnet before brekkie. "My experiences in the Alps," by a lady mountain-climber who's written on the fly-leaf, "To my good friends the Elbridges, in memory of many happy days together at Chamounix. October, 1907." Well, that settles _that_. "Essay on Compensation" in limp leather, by R.W. Emerson, published by Houghton, Mifflin & Co. Oh, righto! Reckoned that'd be over your head, did they? Well, we'll show 'em! We'll read it just out of spite. Open it at the red ribbon:

"Of the like nature is that expectation of change which instantly follows the suspension of our voluntary activity. The terror of cloudless noon--"

Hang on, it must be nearly noon by now! Ten past nine, that's all! Well, nothing for it but to get dressed and go for a wander round the grounds. The bath's out, too noisy. And so, dead careful, almost sneaky about it, you get dressed.
